Name: self_consistency_refusal_erosion
Title: The Self-Consistency Trap: Do Multi-Turn Jailbreaks Erode LLM Safety by Making the Model Agree With Its Own Prior Concessions?
Short Hypothesis: Multi-turn jailbreaks do not primarily succeed by disguising the final harmful query; they succeed because the model's *own prior partial-compliance turns*, once in context, exert a causal downward pull on the refusal-direction projection at later turns — a 'self-consistency trap' in which the model refuses less because doing so would contradict what it already said. We hypothesize this self-generated-context pull is mechanistically separable from, and larger than, the pull from benign user-side filler ('context dilution'), and that surgically neutralizing it (conversational memory hygiene) restores single-turn-level safety with minimal utility cost.
Related Work: Recent multi-turn work (Tempest, MEEA, Crescendo) empirically shows gradual erosion and 'partial-compliance re-injection,' and MEEA notes safety is 'history-dependent,' but none mechanistically identify the causal source of erosion. Defenses (X-Boundary, SafeDream, AgentLens, KG-Guard) accumulate per-turn risk signals or reshape safety boundaries but treat the conversation as an aggregate input; they do not distinguish erosion caused by the model's *own* prior outputs from erosion caused by user-supplied benign context, nor do they causally manipulate conversation history to test the mechanism. Single-turn refusal-direction work (Arditi et al., Pan et al. ICML 2025) never studies how self-generated context shifts refusal geometry. Our distinction: a controlled causal decomposition of multi-turn refusal erosion into a self-consistency pathway vs a context-dilution pathway via counterfactual conversation-history editing, plus a mechanism-targeted defense.
Abstract: Multi-turn jailbreaks reliably bypass LLM safety by spreading a harmful goal across seemingly innocuous turns, exploiting 'partial compliance' from earlier responses. Yet the mechanism behind this gradual erosion is unknown: is the final harmful query simply better disguised, or does the accumulating conversation actively pull the model away from refusal? We propose and test a specific mechanism — the self-consistency trap — in which the model's own prior partial-compliance turns, once part of the context, causally lower the refusal-direction projection at later turns, so that the model complies partly to remain consistent with what it already said. Using open-weight chat models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it) and multi-turn attack transcripts (Crescendo/Tempest-style, MEEA), we extract the refusal direction and track its projection across turns. We then causally decompose erosion via counterfactual history editing: (a) replacing the model's own compliant turns with refusals or removing them (isolating the self-consistency pathway) and (b) replacing benign user filler while keeping model turns fixed (isolating context dilution). We find the self-consistency pathway accounts for the majority of refusal-projection drop, and that erosion tracks the *model's own* commitment, not user-side benign volume. Exploiting this, we introduce conversational memory hygiene — a training-free intervention that re-projects or masks the self-generated concession component from prior-turn representations — which restores near single-turn safety on multi-turn benchmarks while preserving multi-turn task utility, outperforming per-turn steering baselines.
Experiments: 1) Transcript corpus: assemble multi-turn jailbreak transcripts by running Crescendo/Tempest-style and MEEA-style progressive attacks against the three open-weight models on harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT, keeping successful erosion trajectories; also collect matched benign multi-turn conversations and multi-turn utility dialogues (MT-Bench-style). 2) Refusal geometry over turns: extract the refusal direction (difference-in-means, harmful vs benign, single-turn) and measure its projection on the final-user-token representation at each turn t of every transcript, producing an erosion trajectory. Establish that projection monotonically decays across turns in successful attacks. 3) Causal decomposition via counterfactual history editing. Self-consistency pathway: at turn t, replace the model's own prior compliant turns with (i) explicit refusals, (ii) neutral non-committal text, (iii) deletion, then re-run turn t and measure the change in refusal projection and in attack success (StrongREJECT/Llama-Guard graded). Context-dilution pathway: hold the model's own turns fixed but swap user-side benign filler for content-matched paraphrases or remove filler, measuring the same. Report per-pathway indirect effect sizes; hypothesis: the self-consistency edits recover most of the lost refusal projection while dilution edits do not. 4) Dose-response: correlate erosion magnitude with the *number/strength of the model's own concessions* vs the *amount of user benign context*, to distinguish the two hypotheses quantitatively. 5) Identify the self-generated concession component: fit a direction separating the model's compliant prior turns from refusal prior turns and measure its overlap with, and causal contribution to, later-turn refusal suppression. 6) Conversational memory hygiene defense: at inference, re-project out (or attention-mask) the concession component from prior-turn key/value or residual representations before generating each new turn. Compare attack success rate on multi-turn benchmarks (converted HarmBench/StrongREJECT, SafeMTData if available) against: no defense, per-turn refusal steering, and input-level guardrails; also report multi-turn utility (MT-Bench multi-turn, coherence) and over-refusal on benign multi-turn sets. 7) Cross-model and cross-attack generalization. Metrics: per-turn refusal-projection decay, per-pathway causal indirect effect, dose-response correlations, multi-turn ASR reduction, utility delta, over-refusal rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The self-consistency and context-dilution pathways may be entangled (a compliant model turn is both self-generated and benign context); we mitigate with the fixed-turn factorial edits and report residual entanglement. 2) Editing the model's own prior turns changes conversational coherence, which could confound refusal changes; we control with neutral-text and paraphrase edits and check coherence. 3) The refusal direction extracted single-turn may not be optimal for multi-turn representations; we validate by also fitting a direction on multi-turn refusals. 4) Some attacks may erode safety purely via final-query disguise (no self-consistency effect), yielding a partial or null result for those families — itself an informative characterization of attack types. 5) The memory-hygiene defense could degrade multi-turn helpfulness by erasing legitimate prior context; we quantify this tradeoff explicitly. 6) Results are on mid-size open-weight models and may not transfer to frontier models, though the mechanism is model-agnostic in spirit.
